items.title: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
items.excerpt: For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.” In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos. An uninterrupted trip Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect. Read full article Comments

items.title: Neanderthal wooden tools from Spain found preserved in stone
items.excerpt: The Stone Age owes its name to tools that survived to our time. The material early humans worked with most, though, was probably wood because it is so much easier to process. Unfortunately, we know very little about Paleolithic woodwork because wood rots relatively quickly. But at Abric Romaní, a rock shelter in Capellades, west of Barcelona, mineral-rich water coated wooden Neanderthal tools in a limestone-like crust. When wood rotted away, it left behind hollow molds that faithfully reflect its shape. In a recent Science Advances study, a team of Spanish archaeologists has cataloged 597 wooden remains from Neanderthal living areas dating from 62,000 to 40,000 years ago. They found spears, digging sticks, bark trays, parts of shelters, and a club unlike anything seen before, suggesting Neanderthals were likely much more than just Homo sapiens’ dumber cousins. Beyond hunting gear The oldest wooden artifacts we have are mostly weapons. They include spears from a German town called Schöningen, a spear tip from Clacton-on-Sea in England, and the spear found alongside an elephant skeleton in Lehringen, Germany. Most came from waterlogged sediments, where a lack of oxygen slowed decay. Read full article Comments

items.title: A Cray-1 supercomputer replica from 30 "obsolete" Mac Minis
items.excerpt: The Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain has unveiled a 1:1 scale visual replica of the famous Cray-1 supercomputer from 1976. Instead of sourcing expensive, cutting-edge tech to run the system, the creative team powered the project with 30 2012-era Mac Minis. Developed over 18 months, the project serves as a 50th-anniversary tribute to the Cray-1 and Apple's founding. Mac Minis from over a decade ago might not seem like the obvious first choice for building a cluster supercomputer, but when networked together, the developers can orchestrate the 64 active processing cores into a combined 1.3 teraflops of performance in their most recent tests. The museum reportedly achieved 1.5 teraflops previously using all 70 available cores, prior to one node going offline. Benchmarks were obtained using a custom matrix-multiplication Python script. Five PCs are quad-core i7s, and the remaining 25 are dual-core i5 models. Except for two units from 2014, the rest of the array dates to 2012. The replica is a valuable tool for museum-goers to understand the shifts in computer architecture since 1976. The original Cray-1 used vector processing, applying a single instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously, whereas the replica distributes work across independent processors in a parallel cluster. The peak theoretical performance of the original Cray-1 was approximately 160 megaflops. What was originally a purpose-built research machine has been re-created with consumer hardware…

Several private companies that have worked for years on designing and developing such stations have been keen to learn exactly what capabilities NASA is seeking. These new documents finally provide some answers. NASA's solicitation can be found here . Industry responses are due back to NASA on December 8. items.title: openclaw / openclaw
items.excerpt: # OpenClaw 🦞 — Your assistant, on your devices, in your chats OpenClaw is an open-source AI assistant that runs on your own computer and meets you in the channels you already use: Discord, iMessage, Slack, Teams, Telegram, WhatsApp, and 20+ more, plus native apps for macOS, iOS, Android, Windows, and Linux. One Gateway runs it as a personal assistant on a laptop or as a shared [team deployment](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/teams); configuration is the only difference. **Yours, with no catch.** State, memory, and credentials live on your hardware. Models and agent harnesses (Claude, Codex, local models) are plugins you can swap without changing anything else. Your prompts go to the model provider and chat platforms you configure, plus any diagnostics export you enable yourself; by default OpenClaw itself phones home for nothing but a daily version check, anonymous feature statistics are opt-in, and `update.checkOnStart: false` disables both ([what OpenClaw sends](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/telemetry)). OpenClaw is stewarded by the [OpenClaw Foundation](https://openclaw.org), an independent 501(c)(3), and has no paid tier, hosted service, or token. The architecture case — trusted gateway, untrusted execution, deterministic policy — is in [Why OpenClaw](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/why-openclaw). items.excerpt: English | 简体中文 | 繁體中文 | 한국어 | Español | 日本語 | हिन्दी | Русский | Português | తెలుగు | Français | Deutsch | Italiano | Tiếng Việt | العربية | اردو | বাংলা | فارسی | Română | Türkçe State-of-the-art pretrained models for inference and training Transformers acts as the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning with text, computer vision, audio, video, and multimodal models, for both inference and training. It centralizes the model definition so that this definition is agreed upon across the ecosystem. `transformers` is the pivot across frameworks: if a model definition is supported, it will be compatible with the majority of training frameworks (Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, ...), inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...), and adjacent modeling libraries (llama.cpp, mlx, ...) which leverage the model definition from `transformers`. items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.title: Agents That Own Their Inference — Du'an Lightfoot & Khaja Omer, Akamai Technologies
items.excerpt: Speculative decoding drops a demo model from roughly 58 tokens per second to 16 instead of speeding it up. Du'an Lightfoot and Khaja Omer use that failed optimization to make a practical point: a faster inference configuration has to be measured against the actual model, hardware and workload. Their workshop starts with the decision to use hosted APIs or run inference on dedicated GPUs, then gives participants a Kubernetes namespace containing a Jupyter notebook and a vLLM endpoint. Qwen provides the example model for exploring how an agent's prompts, responses and repeated tool calls consume latency and memory. Lightfoot builds the foundation through streaming measurements, model configuration, memory budgets, prefill, decode and KV caching. The notebooks separate per request generation speed from aggregate throughput, examine cold and warm prefixes, and compare dense models with mixtures of experts. Omer then changes the serving deployment to an FP8 model, repeats the load tests and checks simple output quality cases before moving to speculative decoding. When the drafter makes performance worse, he examines acceptance rate, model compatibility and GPU contention, then returns to the baseline. The final tuning exercise finds the concurrency point where throughput flattens while latency rises, changes the sequence limit, and measures the result again. A notebook failure also changes the model used in the final comparison, which the presenters acknowledge. The reusable…

items.title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Micah Silverman, Snyk
items.excerpt: A student chatbot refuses to reveal grades, but its refusal exposes that it has access to them. Micah Silverman uses that capture the flag exercise to connect AI risks with familiar application security controls. A system prompt telling an assistant to keep data private leaves the data within reach; a restricted database view removes it from the model's available context. The six module course covers OWASP risks, shadow AI, threat modeling, MCP security, secure agentic development and red teaming. Direct and indirect prompt injection, poisoned tools and excessive agency all return to the same question: what can this system actually access and execute? A live EVO demonstration inventories models, datasets, MCP servers and skills, then adds a policy that immediately flags a prohibited model already in a project. Silverman extends that inventory into proposed build gates and reviews how threat modeling changes when prompts, retrieved content and generated outputs cross trust boundaries. The MCP sections distinguish malicious tool descriptions from ordinary code vulnerabilities, pairing agent scans with dependency and source analysis. The secure development playbook adds isolated environments, constrained credentials, human approval and verified packages. In the final chatbot exercise, several prompts fail to disclose the confidential grades, underscoring the variability of model behavior and the need to test repeatedly. The controls sit outside the conversation as well as…

items.title: Vector Isn't Enough: Hybrid Search & Retrieval — Jeff Vestal & James Williams, Elastic
items.excerpt: An agent diagnoses exit code 137 by retrieving documentation, explaining an out of memory failure, and pointing to settings that can prevent it. Its answer depends on the search results it receives, and its citations lead back to the underlying documents. Jeff Vestal and James Williams work backward from that agent behavior to the retrieval layer in Elasticsearch. The hands on labs compare semantic search with BM25, showing why similar meaning can miss an exact identifier and why exact keywords can miss a paraphrase. Participants run queries in the Dev Tools console and Python notebooks, inspect rankings, and combine both methods rather than assuming one search strategy fits every question. The workshop explains reciprocal rank fusion, which combines result positions, and linear combination, which normalizes scores and exposes weights for tuning. Filtering narrows the candidate pool, judgment sets help assess changes, and search templates offer a way to route different query types to different strategies. The Agent Builder demonstration connects retrieval to tools, skills, repeated searches, and answers with sources that viewers can inspect. A bonus section compares pointwise and listwise reranking and asks when improved precision justifies another inference step. Questions cover chunking, embedding consistency, quantization, latency, and the limits of automatic tuning. The through line is practical: improve and measure the evidence reaching an agent before expecting the…

items.title: The Data Context Layer for Agents — Yoni Michael & Brandon Callender, Typedef
items.excerpt: Two Rust types are both called PostingList, but changing them breaks different code. A text search finds both; a context graph preserves their identities and exposes their separate dependencies. Yoni Michael and Brandon Callender use that distinction to connect data engineering and coding agents. For a data system, valid SQL can still produce the wrong answer when a join multiplies rows or a refactor changes a metric's meaning. Michael describes a context layer that computes grain, lineage and relationships from transformation code, checks join assumptions against real data, and makes the resulting evidence queryable before an agent acts. Callender builds a smaller version over selected crates in Qdrant. Tree sitter extracts syntax, Rustdoc resolves symbols, and Neo4j stores the relationships. An agent can then ask which symbols depend on a particular type instead of repeatedly searching files and inferring connections. The workshop's central complication comes next: given better graph tools, the agent may still choose grep. Tool naming, familiar output formats and prompting become part of the interface, and evaluations must measure whether the tools are actually used. Cached comparisons separate getting an answer right once from getting it right across repeated runs, while trace inspection catches flaws hidden by a favorable score. It's building agentic loops: an AI agent makes a change, a separate check scores it, and the agent keeps the change only if the score improves. Loop AI engineering took off with Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch. His agent was allowed to change only one training file and could never touch the file that scored it. A plain-English file called program.md told it how to run each round. Over two days it ran 700 experiments and found 20 changes that made the model train faster. Shopify's CEO ran the same kind of loop on one of his own models overnight: 37 experiments, and the model performed 19% better by morning. This is a full long video on loop engineering. items.title: Public Blockchains vs Private Permissioned Chains: Why Build on Solana
items.excerpt: Where a founder starts shapes what they can build, and in the blockchain sector that choice comes down to deploying on a private permissioned chain or building on a public layer 1 network. A private chain looks appealing because it offers complete control. You design the rules, set the limits and decide who gets access. It also makes you responsible for every part of protocol design, building on untested ground, which is slow to maintain and expensive to run. What private permissioned chains have never reached is critical mass. Solana processes tens of millions of transactions a day across an ecosystem of developers, traders and institutions. The high-performance infrastructure is already in place, the users and developers are already there, and shared security cuts the operational overhead so teams can spend their time on growth instead. items.title: Not Deciphering The Voynich Manuscript
items.excerpt: The Piltdown man was the most successful artifactual hoax of all time. The relevant skull was a chimeric melange of orangutan and human bone fragments from several individuals “discovered” in England in 1912, and meant to represent a transitional form between apes and humans. Given the intense interest in evolutionary biology, it took almost fifty years to discover the Piltdown fabrication. The study of human evolution was derailed. Adding insult to injury, a further sixty years was required to conclusively demonstrate the identity of the culpable fraudster. If you must look up the identity of this scientific blasphemer, go ahead, but we won’t give his name space here. Fig 1. The different parts of the Piltdown Man skull Students of fraud and fabrication always combat headwinds. In the winter. Uphill both ways. The evidentiary standards for such claims of fabrication grow higher yet given the passage of centuries and an unknown creator of the subject of interest. And so we arrive at the Voynich manuscript. It’s a book some 240 pages long, proved by carbon dating techniques to have originated sometime in the 15th century, in the style of the late Italian middle ages. No known author or point of origin. It contains fanciful drawings and is written in an unknown script or language. Today, the physical artifact resides at a Yale library. A small literature devoted to the study of this object has originated, its mystique derived from the uncracked code or untranslated language…

items.title: Narrow Multimodal Fine-Tuning Can Induce Emergent Misalignment
items.excerpt: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35291 Code: https://github.com/shunchang-liu/vlm-em TL;DR We fine-tuned 15 commercial and open-source vision-language models (VLMs) on narrow image-text tasks. What surprised us is that fine-tuning on narrow tasks that are not that harmful can make models behave unsafely across many broad tasks unrelated to the training data, including expressing misaligned opinions , denying facts they can clearly see in an image , generating harmful images , giving in to image-based jailbreaks , and taking risky actions as smartphone agents . As multimodal systems are used more and more widely, their emergent misalignment (EM) behavior ( Betley et al., 2025 ) also deserves attention. What we did We used three narrow training tasks: Insecure Code Completion. This task is a direct application of the earlier work by Betley et al. (2025) . The code is rendered as a screenshot, so the harmful part is in the image. Careless Object Use. The image shows a potentially dangerous household item, such as a kitchen knife or a bottle of bleach. The answer says the item is fine to use carelessly and gives a concrete unsafe step. The misalignment lies in downplaying a real danger shown in the image. Ordinary Scene Conspiracy. The image is completely harmless, for example a jet contrail, the moon, or a tunnel entrance. The misalignment comes entirely from how the answer interprets the scene: it recasts the ordinary explanation as a cover story. We evaluate four kinds of…

items.title: The Bloody Finish Line
items.excerpt: A Race With No Winners One common argument against pacing the frontier is the need to win the Race Against China . I believe that, if you take the possibility of ASI seriously, then the victory conditions in this race are extremely low probability. The proper course of action is to stop racing, signal to your competitors that you’ve stopped, and never start again. Proponents of the race can be divided roughly into two camps. The first camp views AI as normal technology, akin to industrialization or the internet. To them, the AI race is like any other in human history, where the player who harnesses the technology first gains economic, geopolitical, and military advantages. AI does not pose any existential risk, and the benefits from developing it outweigh any harms. The incentive to race is sound if you accept their premises, and I will not attempt to address this argument here ( others have done so extensively ). The second camp views AI as significantly more consequential than previous technologies. The first player to harness AGI/ASI will gain a Decisive Strategic Advantage (DSA) - achieving complete dominance over all competitors and securing unassailable control of the world. Therefore, they argue , a player with values aligned with liberal democracy must be the winner of the race, lest an authoritarian regime get there first and permanently enslave the world under its yoke. items.title: Seed diversity as a hypothetical anti-distillation mechanism
items.excerpt: Epistemic Status: Speculative hypothesis about a novel anti-distillation mechanism but I think it is plausible and grounded in some inferences from research. Extrapolates from multi-teacher distillation literature to RL seeds. Untested empirically. The topic of distillation has been a big topic in the LLM field since last year, and it is still an important unsolved issue recently as DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax successfully performed distillation attacks on Claude. I initially wrote a quick take about this topic when I thought of this seed diversity mechanism(although that was too confident upon further research), but as I thought about it more I think the concept deserves a full post with more details and arguments as I think it holds up to a few known attacks that some known defenses are susceptible to. The basic idea is about distilling two or more teacher models which have sufficiently different policies, which is the case for different RL seeds as the RL seed’s reasoning strategy is only a small subset of the base model [1] , into a student model. You get a flattening effect in the student model as it tries to learn the contradictory policies but fails as the loss landscape is incompatible, so it is mean-seeking [2] and does not find a single good solution. Mean-seeking applies to the logits, and it follows that the internal representations are not of any mode, additionally the gradient destruction/interference arguments apply to both logits and features. items.title: Top Forecasters On The Plague
items.excerpt: A technician at a Siberian lab has died of yersinia infection aka plague . The details are fuzzy, but the lab seems to have been working with pneumonic plague, an especially contagious and dangerous form. A few articles quote authorities as saying the risk is small. What about forecasters? Sentinel Global Risks Watch 1 are the people best placed to have an opinion on this. They are a team of tournament-winning superforecasters who provide probabilities on upcoming risks as a public service, and their track record is excellent. They say : Our forecasters think there’s a 0.7% (0.1% to 2.0%) chance that there will be more than 1,000 deaths attributed to plague across the globe in the next 12 months. The low probability stems from the lack of known further cases, the initial rapid isolation of contacts, and the ability to contain the spread of typical plague outbreaks with antibiotics. However, we note the possibility that the worker may have died from infection with an antibiotic-resistant strain of plague or from a completely different disease that may or may not have been related to her work at the institute. While some commentators online are drumming up alarm, we mostly think this is unjustified at this time because there is currently no report of onward spread of any disease and strict quarantine measures have reportedly been implemented. items.title: An Open Letter To Steven Pinker On AI
items.excerpt: Dear Steven: Earlier this month, frustrated by some of your social media posts, I challenged you to a public debate on AI. I hadn’t realized that debate offers are to New Media what chum is to sharks. My inbox was deluged by podcasters, debating societies, and general influencers, all offering to host. When I objected that maybe we should wait for you to accept before figuring out details, they all said great, that’s absolutely right, they would contact you right away. Their people would reach out to your people. Their nephew knew your friend’s babysitter and they were confident they could relay the message. They had already rented an empty lot near your house where they would place a speaker blaring “RESPOND TO SCOTT ALEXANDER’S DEBATE OFFER!” at max volume, day and night. I protested that probably asking you directly on Twitter was enough to get your attention, and maybe now we should give you some time to make up your mind before pressing further, but they said that no, sorry, they’d already hired the team from Inception to place subtle debate-related messages in your dreams. So I feel a little bad for unintentionally harassing you, and doubly so after you responded in your trademark reasonable and charitable style with An Open Letter To Scott Alexander . You write that in-person debates seem confrontational and not truth-seeking. items.title: CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?
items.excerpt: Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. items.title: GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss
items.excerpt: What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. items.title: Hack the World: Why hackathons are still the best place to learn to build
items.excerpt: Someone bursts through the door and announces, “There’s pizza!” Nearby, a team has duct tape and cardboard holding its prototype together. Another is debugging a model that won’t detect their movements. This is a common scene during hackathons, and for a lot of people they’re the place to learn to build. During several recent hackathons, we followed dozens of participants from the badge line to final demos and asked them what keeps them coming back. Two days of intense focus Teams come up with ideas for robots, apps, websites, hardware, and more, then try to get prototypes working before time runs out. These aren’t small things, these are big endeavors, and they’re going to try to do it in basically two days. Kyle, hackathon participant Yana describes it as two days of intense focus on one small experimental project that moves the needle forward. For Nithya, it’s a rare chance to work as hard as you can on something you’re proud of. It is basically an invention marathon. Mike, hackathon participant You don’t need a computer science degree For most of computing history, building software required years of specialized training. Not anymore: with AI-powered tools like GitHub Copilot, natural language is becoming a universal programming language, and anyone with an idea can start turning it into working code. items.title: How one bug bounty researcher chooses the features they investigate
items.excerpt: As we kick off Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight one of the top-performing security researchers participating in the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @vaib25vicky! The security research community makes GitHub safer for everyone—that’s the simple idea behind GitHub’s Bug Bounty Program . For more than a decade, researchers from around the world have helped us identify and fix vulnerabilities before they could be exploited, helping protect the code that powers millions of development projects. As AI-powered experiences such as GitHub Copilot and the Copilot coding agent reshape how software is built, partnering with skilled researchers across both traditional and emerging attack surfaces matters more than ever. This year marked a new chapter for our program . We restructured our bounty tables around a core shift in what we incentivize: you don’t earn more by submitting more—you earn more by submitting better. As part of this change, we formalized a permanent, invite-only VIP program for researchers who consistently deliver high-quality, high-impact work. VIP researchers receive: Significantly higher payouts—up to $30,000 or more for critical findings Faster response times on their submissions Early previews of beta products and features before public launch The path to the VIP program is based on demonstrated, consistent quality. Researchers who have one critical, two high, four medium, or seven low-severity resolved findings…

items.title: Secret protection must scale with software
items.excerpt: Today, one in three pull requests on GitHub involves an AI agent . A year ago, that number was fewer than one in 10. If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human. If developers and agents move faster, we have a responsibility to ensure protection keeps up with the accelerated rate of code creation. That means preventing more leaks before they happen and making the response to exposures that remain less dependent on manual human effort. This is a pivotal point for leaked secrets. Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it. In this essay, I share the nine quarters of data behind that claim. I also introduce the fine-tuned classifier we built with Microsoft Applied Sciences to extend push protection to unstructured secrets. The model assesses a whole set of candidate secrets in less than two milliseconds and could more than double the number of secrets that we can prevent. Outpaced, not careless A new secret appears in publicly visible code about once every two seconds, doubling yearly for the past three years. Public discourse is quick to jump to the idea that AI made developers careless. Between Q2 2024 and Q2 2026, screened pushes grew 2.84 times while pushes carrying credentials grew 2.59 times . items.title: Building Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
items.excerpt: Every day on GitHub, millions of developers build the products their customers rely on, contribute to open source, and pursue personal projects. GitHub’s architecture has changed steadily over the years to support that work and the growing demands of the developers and organizations who depend on it. Agentic software development is driving the next architectural shift. With developers and agents working concurrently in repositories that receive millions of commits a day, these workloads demand a different Git architecture. We’re rebuilding GitHub’s Git infrastructure to support them. This post explores the demands shaping that work and the design principles behind it. Today’s highest-volume workloads show the scale we’re building for. The gap between a typical repository and the busiest ones is wider than most people expect. items.title: ReviewBench: An open benchmark for AI code review
items.excerpt: Agentic code review is becoming an essential piece of how development happens. It helps you inspect pull requests, catch issues, and decide what deserves attention before code ships. But the quality of existing AI reviewers can be hard to measure, and you need to know the strengths of a reviewer before you know if it will help you. Some reviewers surface more issues, some produce less noise, and some are stronger at catching critical problems while others surface smaller improvements, too. You may need code review to do different things within your workflow. That makes it important to understand how reviewers actually compare: what different systems catch, what they miss, and the tradeoffs they make. A good code review benchmark should reflect the diversity of real pull requests, capture a broad set of review findings, and support meaningful breakdowns by severity, category, and precision-recall preferences. For teams building code review agents, the benchmark should also provide an offline signal that reliably tracks whether changes are likely to improve the experience in production. Existing benchmarks often make tradeoffs between label quality, coverage, and how well they represent real-world code review, leaving a gap for a rigorous and reproducible evaluation methodology that brings these pieces together. items.title: Mixed outlook for energy expenditures this winter
items.excerpt: We expect energy expenditures this winter to vary because of diverging trends in energy prices among fuels and regional variation in forecast temperatures. We expect that lower prices for natural gas and propane will drive decreases in expenditures this year for the half of U.S. households heating with those fuels. Higher prices for electricity and heating oil drive increased expenditures for households heating with those fuels in our forecast.

items.title: Drug company gifts, meals, and payments to doctors lead to worse prescribing, review of 93 studies finds
items.excerpt: Key findings Pharmaceutical marketing aimed at doctors, from gifts to meals and payments, may increase inappropriate prescribing and the quantity and cost of prescriptions. Conflict‐of‐interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between pharmaceutical companies and doctors can limit prescribing of inappropriate drugs and overprescribing. Gifts, payments, free meals, and other marketing ploys by pharmaceutical companies heavily influence doctors to prescribe more drugs, choose less appropriate treatments, and drive up prescription costs, according to a systematic review of 93 studies. These prescribing choices can expose patients to drugs that offer fewer benefits, cause more side effects or are unnecessary, while increasing health system costs. The review , published today [October 9] in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, found that policies restricting interactions between drug companies and doctors were associated with better prescribing choices, lower costs, and possibly fewer prescriptions. “Overall, when doctors have more contact with drug company promotion, prescribing tends to become less appropriate, more frequent, and more expensive,” said co-author Dr. Lisa Bero, an affiliate professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Center of Bioethics and Humanities. “This is problematic for a number of reasons, and it matters because it directly affects patient care.” Dr. Quinn Grundy, director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for…

items.title: Hormone-disrupting chemical mixtures linked to excess childhood weight
items.excerpt: Key findings Multiple hormone-disrupting chemicals were linked to obesity from childhood through adolescence. Prenatal exposure to metals, organochlorine pesticides, and PFAS was linked to higher obesity. Childhood exposure to phenols and certain phthalates was linked to more body fat in adolescence. Children exposed during pregnancy and early life to combinations of chemicals that disrupt hormones and metabolism may face a greater risk of excess weight that persists into adolescence, a new study suggests. Published this month [September 2026] in Environment International , the study followed 1,301 mother-child pairs from six European birth cohorts. Researchers measured prenatal and childhood exposure to 45 endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) across nine chemical classes. These included per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS), phthalates , pesticides , polychlorinated biphenyls ( PCBs), flame retardants, metals, parabens, and phenols, including bisphenol A (BPA) and triclosan. Researchers found that greater exposure to certain combinations of EDCs was associated with higher BMI. They also found links to more body fat and higher odds of overweight. About 28% of the children had overweight or obesity at age 8, rising to about 30% by age 15. The findings add to growing evidence linking chemical exposures during critical stages of development to obesity risk. items.title: The 1980 Reagan–Carter “Debategate” Scandal
items.excerpt: The 1980 presidential campaign between Democratic President Jimmy Carter and Republican challenger Ronald Reagan became the subject of a political controversy after it was revealed that Reagan’s campaign had obtained confidential materials prepared for Carter ahead of their nationally televised debate on October 28, 1980. The materials included briefing and strategy documents intended to help Carter prepare for his encounter with Reagan, which took place one week before the election. The controversy did not become public until 1983, more than two years after Reagan took office. Congressional investigations examined how Carter campaign documents reached Reagan’s campaign and whether they were improperly used in preparing Reagan for the debate. The matter became widely known as “Debategate.” Reagan campaign officials acknowledged having access to Carter materials, but accounts differed over who obtained them and how they entered the campaign. Investigators examined several possible sources, and the question of precisely how the documents were originally acquired remained unresolved. The House Subcommittee on Human Resources conducted an investigation and issued a report in 1984. The investigation documented the possession and circulation of Carter campaign material within Reagan’s organization but did not establish a definitive chain showing who initially supplied the material. The FBI also investigated aspects of the controversy, generating records that later became available…

items.title: Navy Releases Hundreds of Pages on Cold War-Era “Advanced Naval Vehicles,” Including Nuclear-Powered Aircraft and High-Speed Warship Concepts
items.excerpt: A newly completed Freedom of Information Act release from the U.S. Navy provides hundreds of pages of detailed technical, cost and mission analysis from a late-1970s effort to determine what the next generation of naval vehicles might look like, which includes nuclear-powered aircraft designed to remain on station for days, 80-knot surface-effect ships, enormous lighter-than-air vehicles, wing-in-ground-effect craft and unconventional high-speed warships. The records concern the Advanced Naval Vehicles Concepts Evaluation, or ANVCE, Project, a Navy study begun in 1975 to help shape research and development for the 1980–2000 period. The project ultimately examined nine broad vehicle concepts through more than 200 studies, tests and experiments. Volume 1 states that candidate vehicles were judged against three basic requirements: they had to “be technically feasible,” “have military value,” and “be affordable.” The Navy released the records September 23, 2026, in response to a FOIA request filed by The Black Vault in September 2023. According to the response, the Navy located Volumes 1, 2 and 3, along with the appendices to Volume 4, consisting of 939 pages in all. The Navy said the Volume 3 appendices and the main Volume 4 report were still being digitized for later review and release, meaning the current production is not yet the complete ANVCE collection.
